title: 18. The Shape of the Prayer Itself
purpose: It assembles, from named Ismaili juridical and da'i sources, the obligations, minimums, sunnahs and disqualifying defects of the ritual prayer, together with a warning treatise on those who neglect it.

points.text: The question-and-answer book reports that Ali (ع) recited 'So be patient; the promise of God is true' during prayer not as the opening of that surah but specifically to silence and rebuke Ibn al-Kawwa, who kept raising his voice.

In the madhhab of the Ahl al-Bayt, the long portions of al-mufassal run from al-Hujurat to al-Mujadila, the middle from al-Mujadila to 'Amma yatasa'alun', and the short from 'Amma yatasa'alun' to al-Nas.

The same source lists acts that break the covenant, including abandoning prayer or prescribed works without excuse, disbelieving a believer's oath after accusing him, fornication, killing a believer, reviling the summoner or his appointee, and refusing the summoner's call to strive with person and wealth.

Per Mukhtasar al-Musannaf, if the intention for prayer slips away — through preoccupation, forgetfulness or anything else — before one enters the prayer, the prayer afterwards does not suffice; and one may not recite inwardly what the tongue has not uttered.
On the tashahhuds, performing the first does not excuse one from the second, but the second does suffice in place of the first.

Al-Ikhtisar gives the minimum by which prayer is completed as five limits — opening takbir, standing for the able, bowing, prostration, and sitting for the tashahhud — valid for one who forgot or did not know more, whereas one who knows the limits and deliberately omits any obligation or sunnah has no prayer and must repeat it, and the ignorant man is obliged to learn.

Postural rulings are specified by source: the woman places her hands above her knees on her thighs so as not to raise her hindquarters (al-Akhbar); those behind the imam answer 'Our Lord, to You belongs all praise' quietly, except the appointed relayer who raises his voice with it and the takbir but not the tasbih (Tawil al-Daaim); and the sitter folds his left leg beneath him and keeps the right upright (Tawil al-Daaim, outward sense).

In the jurisprudential exchange between Shaykh Hasan ibn Mawla Adam al-Hindi and the sayyids of Yemen, the prayer of a woman who has not undergone khafd is valid and intimacy with her is permissible, and likewise for the man, though the sunnah is to hasten to it.

Jafar ibn Sulayman, in al-Sayf al-Aqta fi Ibtal al-Bida addressed to the people of Yemen, rebukes those who profess walaya yet never prostrate in a single rakah, citing the Prophet's 'between the servant and unbelief is abandoning the prayer' and Ali's 'there is no portion in Islam for one who abandons the prayer' to conclude that such a person holds no share of Islam.

Jafar ibn Sulayman divides the neglecters of prayer into two kinds — people of tribal temper absorbed in themselves with animal nature dominant, and people of arrogance and coarse insolence, especially the women — and holds both kinds to be found in every school of Islam and every religion, adding that even unbelievers, including those of India, perform some inherited worship, so that such arrogance falls under the Quranic threat against those too proud to worship God, the path on which Iblis perished.

Jafar ibn Sulayman argues that worship benefits only the worshipper, God having no need of it, since He created jinn and mankind to worship Him for their own benefit, and that no one has a claim of walaya to the friends of God except by holding fast to the hem of the prayer.

The lists of obligations differ by source: Tawil al-Shariah gives seven — first takbir, recitation, bowing, prostration, tasbih, greeting, taslim — while the Dai Zayd ibn Muhammad ibn al-Fadl gives seven as intention, first takbir, standing, recitation, bowing, prostration, taslim, and the Majalis al-Mustansiriyya gives intention, turning to the qibla, takbirat al-ihram, recitation of the Opening, bowing, prostration, and sitting for the salutation.

Tawil al-Shariah forbids moving the foot or speaking from the opening takbir to the taslim, cites the Prophet on prostrating upon seven members, and prohibits reciting while bowing, disturbing pebbles, turning like a fox, squatting like a monkey, pecking like a crow, and drooping the head below the level of the back.

Zayd ibn Muhammad ibn al-Fadl gives the prayer four limits — place, time, purity, intention — with five daily prayers of seventeen rakahs divided into obligation and sunnah, and interprets 'the one who abandons my sunnah is cursed' esoterically to mean the one who abandons my legatee is banished from God's mercy, adding that the outward prayer itself neither forbids nor commands.

The Majalis al-Mustansiriyya enumerates seven obligatory prayers (residence of seventeen rakahs, travel of eleven, Friday requiring four with the imam, fear, the tawaf of obligatory Hajj, the tawaf of obligatory Umrah, and the prayer over the bier which binds every Muslim who knows until one undertakes it) and twelve sunnah prayers, matching purity's divisions to the clauses and letters of the shahada.

The Majalis al-Mustansiriyya lists twelve sunnahs within each of the five prayers, ending with the rule that any prayer lacking a first sitting has a qunut counted in its place, while any prayer with two tashahhud sittings has no qunut.

Ali's Four Hundred Etiquettes forbids clasping the hands while standing in prayer as resembling the People of the Book, rules that gross turning about cuts off the prayer and requires beginning again with adhan, iqama and takbir, and directs sitting between the two prostrations until the limbs are still, turning to the right on leaving the prayer, and making oneself hear the recitation when praying alone.

Answering Muhammad Ali ibn Salih al-Badri of India, the master Hibat Allah rules that since no text from the friends of God forbids reciting the two surahs of refuge in obligatory prayer, such a prayer is complete — one who recited al-Nas in the first rakah repeats it in the last, one who recited al-Ikhlas in the first recites al-Falaq in the second — but one should not deliberately recite in this manner, putting it in the position of the sunnah.
